playground.title: Enemy AI Prototype
playground.shortDescription: Personal Experiment • C++ AI behavior sandbox — pathfinding, wandering and interactive seek behaviors with SDL2

content.title: Project Philosophy
content.text: **Enemy AI Prototype** is my personal playground for exploring AI programming with **C++**, **SDL2**, and **CMake**. It's both a **learning lab** where I experiment with different AI behaviors and a **showcase** of what I've figured out so far. I'm really focused on keeping the code clean and readable if someone else (or future me ahahah) looks at this, they should be able to understand what's happening.

content.title: Pathfinding Implementation
content.text: The heart of the project is a **custom A* pathfinding algorithm** that I built from scratch. I studied the theory and then adapted it to work exactly how I needed it to. The pathfinding lets entities navigate complex environments efficiently, and building it taught me a lot about **graph theory**, **heuristic algorithms**, and how to optimize things for real-time applications.

content.title: AI Behavior Systems
content.text: I've implemented several different AI behaviors that feel natural: **Wander behavior** makes entities move around randomly but in a way that looks organic rather than robotic; **Patrol systems** let them follow specific routes with smooth transitions between waypoints; **Seek behavior** makes entities chase targets (like your mouse cursor) with realistic acceleration and deceleration.

content.title: Technical Architecture
content.text: I'm using **SDL2** for graphics and input handling, and the whole thing demonstrates what I've learned about modern **C++ programming** - **object-oriented design**, **memory management**, and building things in a modular way. Using **CMake** means it builds cleanly on different platforms, which is something you really need to know for professional C++ work.

content.title: Continuous Development
content.text: This project keeps **evolving** as I learn new AI concepts and improve my existing code. Each time I come back to it, I focus on making the **code better**, **performance faster**, and **adding new features**. This iterative approach has taught me a lot about **maintaining software**, **using version control properly**, and how to improve things incrementally rather than trying to rebuild everything from scratch.

content.title: Code Quality Standards
content.text: One thing I really care about is keeping the **code clean, readable, and well-documented**. I want to write code that doesn't just work, but that someone else could look at and learn from. This focus on quality has really improved my **software engineering practices** and how I communicate technical ideas.

content.title: Future Plans
content.text: The modular design makes it easy to add new AI behaviors and systems. I'm planning to add **flocking algorithms**, **finite state machines**, **neural network integration**, and **multi-agent coordination**. This forward-thinking approach is part of my commitment to **continuous learning** and developing my AI skills.

playground.title: Motion Overlay
playground.shortDescription: Personal Experiment • Webcam face & hand tracking with an icon overlay that reacts to your expression and gesture, entirely on-device with MediaPipe

content.title: Project Philosophy
content.text: **Motion Overlay** is a small on-device computer vision experiment: it tracks your face and hands through the webcam and drops an icon on top of each one, live, directly in the browser. The icon isn't static either — it reacts to what you're actually doing: **smile, wink, or look surprised** and the face icon follows; make a **fist, thumbs up, peace sign, or point** and the hand icon follows that too. No frame is ever uploaded anywhere — every bit of it runs locally as **WebAssembly**.

content.title: Why On-Device Tracking
content.text: I wanted to get hands-on with **computer vision that doesn't need a server**. Streaming webcam frames to a backend for inference is the easy path, but it's slower, it costs money per user, and it means someone else's camera feed is leaving their machine. Running the models client-side with **MediaPipe Tasks Vision** answered all three: instant feedback, zero infrastructure, and the video never leaves the tab.

content.title: Reading Expressions & Gestures
content.text: Under the hood this uses MediaPipe's **FaceLandmarker** (with blendshapes turned on) and **GestureRecognizer**, two pre-trained models compiled to WebAssembly. Blendshapes are ARKit-style scores like *mouthSmileLeft* or *jawOpen* — I threshold a handful of them to pick between a smile, a laugh, a wink, surprise, a frown, or a pucker. The gesture model classifies each hand directly into a fixed set: **fist, open palm, thumbs up/down, peace sign, pointing, or "I love you"** — it isn't something I trained, Google ships it pre-built into the same package.

content.title: Making It Feel Alive
content.text: Raw landmark coordinates jitter a lot frame-to-frame, so each icon's position is **smoothed with an exponential lerp** rather than snapping straight to the detection, and a recognized expression or gesture has to **hold for a few consecutive frames** before the icon actually switches — otherwise a single misread frame makes it flicker. The video and the icons are mirrored together as a single unit for a natural selfie view, while the icon glyphs themselves are counter-flipped so they never render backwards.

content.title: Respecting the Camera
content.text: Camera access is never requested automatically. The experience opens on a plain **"Enable camera"** step with a short explanation of what happens to the feed (nothing — it never leaves the browser), so the permission prompt is always a direct result of an explicit choice, not something sprung on you the moment the page loads.

experience.instructions: Enable your camera, then try a fist, thumbs up, peace sign, or a big smile — the icon on your face and hands reacts to what it sees.
